extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and special principles for construing letters-patent: how Claims, the specification, drawings, models, contemporaneous filings, and external facts are to be read and balanced to determine the scope of a patent. Includes general maxims (ordinary meaning, liberal construction for pioneers) and many specific doctrines (combinations, function/result claims, reissues, foreign words, 'substantially as described', etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and related parts interpret the Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire specification, with the drawings, model, oath, and title, are to be considered as interpreting the Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations contained in the specification are to be taken as the inventor's own interpreter of the meaning of his Claim and of the essential qualities of the invention protected by his patent; the whole specification may and should be looked at to learn from the description of the invention (cases cited: Mathews v. Iron Clad Mfg. Co., Ex parte Holt, Bruce v. Mader, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and explicit Claim language controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Claim is clear and explicit its language controls its meaning, without referring to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If terms are clear, the claim must be construed by its words; the specification cannot enlarge a clear claim (cites Rich v. Close).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents construed liberally to sustain inventor's rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are to be construed liberally, so as to sustain and not destroy the right of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole of the specification may be consulted to cure and sustain the patentee's rights; liberal construction aims to protect the inventor within legitimate linguistic bounds (Francis v. Mellor and other authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubtful specifications may be aided by affidavit or other matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the construction of the patent and specification as to the subject of the grant is doubtful, the affidavit (or other contemporaneous explanatory material) may be resorted to to explain the ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly proper for restraining general expressions in the specification; courts may consider whole specification and external explanatory evidence (Pettibone v. Derringer, Ransom v. Mayor of New York).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be consistent with inventor's oath; whole specification considered where technical terms need explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath and the specification should be consistent; the drawings and model should be considered and the whole specification consulted where words are technical or need explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When terms need explanation in technical sense (e.g., before a jury), it is proper to refer to whole specification and consider it in connection (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may be restricted by the descriptive parts but never enlarged
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing Claims by descriptive portions, the scope of the Claims may often be restricted, but can never be enlarged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be limited to the invention communicated to the public; liberal construction requires interpreting other patent parts broadly but cannot expand Claims beyond what the description legitimately supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: General words limited by the real nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: General words in a description or Claim are to be limited by the real nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Claim's generality is trimmed by the actual invention described in the specification and by the real nature and purpose of the invention (Fischer v. Hayes and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: A general Claim is limited to the invention described in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A general Claim will be limited to the invention described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a Claim may read broadly, it is confined to the invention as described; inventor may abandon parts of described matter and Claims cannot be stretched beyond the described disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are not necessarily limited by drawings when specification shows broader invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are not limited by drawings when the specification shows that the real invention was broader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification demonstrates a broader conception, drawings do not confine the Claim to the precise figures shown (Hamilton v. Ives example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and phrases to be interpreted in their ordinary sense at the patent date
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the contrary appears, a word has its ordinary meaning; meaning is that at the date of the patent, not subsequent changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a word had varied meanings, take it as including only the acts or things to which it then referred; see McDougall v. Eames and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical terms and terms known in the art are given their art-meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms known in the art are to be understood as used in the art rather than broader or more recent meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation depends on the art's usage and the inventor's likely meaning in context (cases cited: Root v. Lamb, Day v. Cary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words interpreted according to inventor's intent as shown by specification and correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are interpreted according to the intent of the inventor, as indicated by their use in the specification, the art, or correspondence with the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will seek inventor's intent from specification text and contemporaneous documents; arrangement of words is less important than purport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous or unintelligible words may be rejected as surplusage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous words, if capable of no intelligible construction and the object of the patent can be made clearly known without them, may be rejected as surplusage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguous terms do not add to understanding the invention, treat them as surplus (cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: When Claim requires no explanation, use ordinary meaning; otherwise investigate history and art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Claim requires no explanation, the court expounds it by the ordinary meaning of its words. If explanation is required, the entire field of inquiry (history of the art, inventor statements, other facts) is open to determine the true invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim ambiguous, seek what the plaintiffs claimed as their invention by looking to specification and external evidence of the inventor's view (Rich v. Close; other notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pioneer patents construed liberally to protect original conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A pioneer patent, introducing an art or instrument entirely new, must be interpreted as liberally as its language will permit to protect the original conception in its widest form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if specification contains specific details, the pioneer patent is not confined to them if a liberal construction can fairly be applied (cases: Kirk v. DuBois, Hammershlag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issued patents may be aided by original specification and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent, if ambiguous and uncertain in itself, may be aided by referring to the specifications, drawings, and model of the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original patent material can be used to construe reissue and to interpret new matter only to the extent it could properly have appeared in the original (Bussey v. Wager; Reedy v. Scott; Schillinger v. Cranford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents granted by special act of Congress limited to inventor's representations
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent granted by special act of Congress, upon representations made by the inventor as to the real nature of his invention, must be limited to the invention as thus represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Congress granted a patent after representations, the patent is confined to what the patentee represented to Congress (Union Mfg. Co. v. Lounsbury and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims construed broadly to support the combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a combination is to be construed liberally in order to support the combination, even though another Claim is made for a special arrangement of the same elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But limitations imposed by inventor (especially after rejection) act as disclaimers and must be strictly construed in favor of the public; if a combination is shown old, claim may be read as covering particular elements employed (Be parte Marsh; Sargent v. Hall; other cites).

rubrics_metrics.name: A combination Claim includes everything expressed or necessarily implied to be material
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a combination includes everything which is either expressed or necessarily implied to be material to the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claimed elements are regarded as material in construing the patent; however, if a claimed element is expressly disclaimed, the claim cannot be construed to cover it (Thompson v. Gildersleeve; Shaver v. Skinner Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot eliminate an expressly claimed element or treat a claimed useless element as immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts cannot, by construction, eliminate a claimed element of a combination simply because it is practically useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimed elements must be treated as material; construction cannot excise a claimed element on the ground of practical uselessness (Williams v. Stolzenbach and authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims for principles/forces interpreted as claims for the instrument or operation applying them
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for the principle or force employed in an invention will be interpreted, if possible, as a Claim for the instrument or operation by which the force is applied to its appropriate object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts prefer to limit abstract principle claims to concrete means/devices when specification indicates such; see Union Paper Bag Co. v. Nixon and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims construed to cover the device performing the function
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a function, where the specification describes the device or apparatus which performs it, will be construed as intended to cover such apparatus or device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional language is read in light of the specification's described means; use cases: Albany Steam Trap Co. v. Felthousen and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result/effect claims construed as means if specification supports
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for a result or effect will be considered as a Claim for the means by which the effect is produced, if the specification, as a whole, is open to that interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes means for achieving the result, the claim can be read as limited to those means (Palmer v. Galling Gun Co.; Henderson v. Cleveland Co-operating Stove Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: A Claim for an entirety (multi-part instrument/process) is not divisible by construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for an entire instrument or process consisting of several steps or divisible parts cannot usually be divided by construction so as to cover the independent members separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless the specification indicates the inventor intended separate claims for parts, a whole claim stands as a unit (National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern R.R. Co.; Evans v. Kelly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two separate Claims cannot be construed together as one to support each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Two apparently separate Claims cannot be construed as one Claim and be thus supported by each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim must stand on its own terms; courts will not merge separate claims to save invalid ones (Seymour v. McCormick and related citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign words and non-English phrases interpreted by context and inventor's object
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign words occurring in a patent are to be interpreted by the context and the real object of the inventor, and to receive such meaning as will effect his intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret foreign terms in light of the specification and the inventor's apparent purpose (White v. Allen and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Substantially as described' and 'as herein described' refer to the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'substantially as described' (and similar phrases like 'as herein described') in the Claim signifies much or little as the patentee evidently designed and refers the Claim to the specification for fuller statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such phrases are always supposed incorporated and relate only to material features of the invention; they enable a claim that on its face covers only a function/result to be construed by the described means (Seymour v. Osborne, Matthews v. Schoneberger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and names construed in connection with specification and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and terms used by the patentee are to be construed in view of the entire specification and drawings; the title should agree with the specification but does not control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title is taken in connection with the specification and drawings and is given a liberal construction; title alone does not control claim scope (Foye v. Nichols; Goodyear v. Railroad examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings construed by the specification; drawings cannot change the character of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings are to be construed by the specifications; but drawings cannot be used to change the character of the invention described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings may aid or illustrate, and may be interpreted by the model, but they cannot be used to alter the descriptive disclosure; they can also demonstrate that the claimed machine is not the one for which it issued in some cases (Burrall v. Jewett; Hancock Inspirator Co. v. Jenks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of words fixed at date of invention; contemporary common knowledge informs reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of a patent is to be construed by its meaning at the date of the patent, not by that subsequently acquired; specification is read in the light of common knowledge unless contrary appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names and terms are interpreted by the evidence of their meaning at the time used; courts look to how words were understood contemporaneously (McDougall v. Eames; McCloskey v. DuBois).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot be enlarged by correspondence or proceedings before the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claims of a patent cannot be enlarged by the correspondence of the inventor with the Patent Office, nor by the proceedings pending the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the specification may aid construction, the claims remain limited to what was legitimately communicated and cannot be expanded by subsequent prosecution history beyond that disclosure (general principle stated in the treatise).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Generic' and 'manufacture' terms are relative and context-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'generic' is relative — same invention may be generic with respect to some inventions and specific to others; the word 'manufacture' may denote the article made or the means by which it is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret these terms according to the nature of the operation or instrument and the position of such instrument/operation in the relevant art; context controls.
